summary: Atlanticism advocates close political, economic and defence cooperation between North America and Europe, institutionalised above all in NATO and rooted in the 1941 Atlantic Charter, with a stress on shared democracy, individual liberty and the rule of law. Its early thinkers, notably Clarence Streit, proposed going further, to a federal union of the Atlantic democracies. It is chiefly a foreign-policy and security outlook, so its own sources are silent on most domestic questions.
scope: The Atlanticist tradition as the defining scholarship and the Streit Council describe it: the Atlantic-community idea from the late 19th century through Lippmann and Streit, the 1941 Atlantic Charter and the 1949 North Atlantic Treaty. It answers only from those texts and from Streit's Union Now, which the scholarship ties to it. It excludes the positions of the parties, governments and adherents who hold it, and continental projects that distance Europe from the US.
